President, Haiti's path to lasting peace and stability rests on unified actions by the Haitians themselves and all the partners, including this Council. The people of Haiti have waited too long for a peaceful future and an opportunity to spend their lives in an environment free from violence and instability. And SRS G. I would like to thank the Special.

Representative of the Secretary-General, Carlos Reis Massieu, and the Special Representative for the Gang Suppression Force, Jack.

Christofides, for their reports.

I would like to give a special.

Welcome to His Excellency the Prime Minister Alex Didier Fisseme and to all the delegations that have joined us today.

Institutionality, as well as the rule.

My country calls upon the security sector in Haiti, including the gang suppression force, to strictly comply with the most rigorous human rights standards, due diligence, and accountability. The protection of the civilian population should be the lodestar of any operation.

President, I thank RSSG Masseur and Special Representative Christa Fidesz for their briefings and welcome the Interim Prime Minister of Haiti and the representatives of the Dominican Republic, Trinidad and Tobago, Kenya and OIF to today's meeting. The multiple crises in Haiti has dragged on for a long time, Haiti's slow political progress, complex and severe security situation, weak national governance, and deteriorating economic and humanitarian conditions have severely hampered its stable development and seriously undermined the confidence of its people and the international community in the country's future. Consolidating signs of progress and breaking the vicious cycle of crisis require a comprehensive approach that addresses both symptoms and root causes. I'd like to make four points. First, there's a need to restore political stability at an early date. The fundamental solution to the Haitian crisis lies in advancing a Haitian-owned and Haitian-led political process, with the country itself assuming primary responsibility for its governance. For many years, the political transition in Haiti has seen multiple setbacks. The goals of forming a legitimate government and restoring political stability have yet to be achieved. We hope that all parties in the country demonstrate firm political will, strengthen unity and cooperation, take substantive steps in areas such as political dialogue and election preparation, create favorable conditions for enhancing governance capacities and stabilizing the chaotic situation, and prevent further delay in the political transition. We support BINU and CARICOM, among others, in continuing to provide assistance in this regard. Second, there's a need to effectively improve security situation. The complex security situation in Haiti means that the authorities should strengthen security governance in earnest and create and effectively implement long-term strategies to reduce violence and prevent gang recruitment, among others. The Secretary General's report expresses concern over civilian casualties resulting from law enforcement operations. Haiti's security sector should further strengthen the protection of civilians, in particular children and other vulnerable groups. Any international security support must respect Haiti's sovereignty, strictly comply with international law, and exercised the utmost caution in the use of force. China's taken note of the progress in the deployment of the relevant international forces and hopes that the country leading the forces will act responsibly toward the Haitian people, this council, and the international community, maintain transparency in specific operations, and promptly brief the Security Council so that this council can maintain close attention and rigorous oversight. Third, there's a need to focus on enhanced Enhancing arms control, the continued flow of illegal arms and ammunition into the hands of guns is a major cause of the never-ending violence in Haiti. Cutting off the flow of arms and ammunition at the source is the only way to effectively prevent gun violence from harming innocent civilians and ensure that external security support can play an effective role. We urge the international community, in particular the main source country of arms and ammunition to strictly implement the Council's arms embargo. We call on the Haitian authorities to strengthen the control of arms and ammunition and expect continued assistance from regional countries and agencies such as UNODC. The Sanctions Committee and this Council should enhance oversight of relevant progress. Fourth, there is a need to keep investing more in people's livelihoods. Underdevelopment and dire living conditions are key root causes of Haiti's prolonged instability. The country's socio-economic conditions continue to deteriorate, with 60 percent of its people living below the poverty line. This drives a large number of people, especially youth and children, to join gangs out of desperation. China calls on the Haitian authorities to increase investment in development to strengthen basic public services, help its people secure basic necessities such as food, education, employment, and health care, and create conditions to enhance its endogenous drivers for self-sustained development. We support the UN, international financial institutions, regional organizations, and others in assisting the country to restore development, improve livelihoods, and eliminate the conditions that breed violence. President, China commends RSG Masure for leading BINU in overcoming difficulties and carrying out its work proactively. We look forward to the continued assistance by BINU to help Haiti in effectively addressing its multiple crises. Ultimately, the key to resolving the Haitian crisis lies in the hands of the Haitian people. China is ready to work with the international community to play a constructive role in helping the Haitian people emerge from the crisis and achieve long-term peace and stability at an early date. Thank you, President.
I thank the representative of China for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Latvia.

Thank you, Madam. First and foremost, I would like to wish a warm welcome to the Prime Minister of Haiti, Mr. Alex Didier Fils-Aime. And I would also like to wish a warm welcome to Mr. Carlos Ruiz-Mercier, SRSG, and Mr. Jack Christophides, Special Representative for the Gang Suppression Force, for their detailed briefings. Madam, we welcome the peaceful transition of power in Haiti in February, and we welcome the establishment of the Council of Ministers that has five female ministers under the leadership of Prime Minister Fisselme. While armed groups continue to dispute territory and to attack the Haitian population, and the humanitarian crisis worsens, institutional continuity and inclusive national dialogue are crucial for the legitimacy of the political process and the re-establishment of public trust. We also welcome the adoption of the National Pact for stability and the organization of elections in Haiti. This brings together a broad group of stakeholders and reflects political consensus. In the future, the commitments laid out in the pact require effective implementation, as underscored by SRSG Mr. Mercier. In order to ensure free, fair, safe and inclusive elections in Haiti, strengthening security measures and the electoral process must continue in parallel. Such an approach should enable Haitians to ensure their names are on electoral registers, to campaign and to vote in safety. This is crucial for legitimate, credible electoral results. We take note of the information, according which the election calendar may be postponed to August. Whilst the safety of candidates and voters is crucial, Haiti must re-establish constitutional order as quickly as possible, and it is highly desirable for the first round of elections to take place before the end of the year. We would encourage the Haitian Government to continue preparing for a reasonable electoral budget that matches the other urgent national needs, and to implement the electoral operational plan without delay. Whilst the homicide rate in Haiti is one of the highest in North America, in America rather, in the world, and gang violence continue to destroy and devastate Haitian lives, we do welcome the establishment of UNSO in Haiti. This is an important step that enables the deployment as well of the Gang Suppression Force.

We have entrusted GSF with a responsibility of exceptional magnitude and historic significance. We expect the GSF to carry out its mandate with effectiveness, accountability, transparency, and in close coordination with national authorities and international partners. While intensified anti-gang operations have led to some important security gains during the reporting period, we encourage all stakeholders to ensure that any use of lethal force is rigorously assessed and proportionate to prevent civilian harm. We recall the importance of compliance with international human rights law and international humanitarian law, including the principles of distinction and proportionality at all times. This means integrating gender and child protection expertise into planning and operations. We emphasize that Bino's support to the GSF in safeguarding human rights must remain strong and consistent, even if at times it seems to be a highly complicated task. We condemn in strongest possible terms the ongoing human rights violations in Haiti, particularly against women and children. It is imperative that the perpetrators committing targeted killings, extortion, gender-based sexual violence, and child trafficking for recruitment and exploitation are brought to justice. Success in combating impunity largely depends on the effectiveness of cooperation between the Haitian National Police and the Haitian judicial system. Law enforcement action must be matched by credible investigations, timely prosecutions, and fair adjudication, ensuring that arrests lead to convictions grounded in full respect of due process. And we acknowledge the progress made in the ongoing operationalization of two specialized judicial units for the investigation and prosecution of crimes, including mass killings and sexual violence, financial crimes, and corruption. Let me recall that widespread corruption is one of the most serious structural causes of a weak state and gang violence in Haiti and needs to be tackled consistently at all levels of the governance structures. We welcome the Haitian government's decision to reactivate the National Commission for Disarmament, Dismantlement and Reintegration and BINUH's immediate outreach to its counterpart to provide technical advice on addressing gang violence. UNVINO and the UN Country Team can provide valuable guidance in supporting the development of a national DDR strategy. Moving forward, to sustain security gains over the long term, it is of utmost importance that the national DDR strategy and implementation processes are effective. Only a solid, dedicated, comprehensive long-term DDR strategy, timely implemented, will put an end to recurring gang and community violence in Haiti. Child protection must remain an immediate priority under DDR, as approximately half of those associated with the gangs are children, who first and foremost should be seen as victims of trafficking, recruitment, and exploitation. And we emphasize the role of the handover protocol established by the UN and Haitian authorities in 2024, and the need for full and consistent implementation as key to protecting children. Finally, at this decisive time for Haiti, Latvia continues to fully support BINUH in its work to foster inclusive political dialogue, strengthen institutions and rule of law, and promote governance grounded in accountability and respect for human rights for the Haitian people to finally live in security and dignity. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Latvia for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Greece.

Madame President, at the outset, I would like to thank SRS Jean-Marcieu and GSF Special Representative Christofidis for their briefings. I also welcome the presence of His Excellency Alix Didier Fisseme, the Prime Minister of Haiti, in the meeting. The full establishment of the UN Support Office in Haiti and the gradual deployment of the GAG Suppression Force should mark a turning point, with a focus on stabilizing the security environment and dismantling criminal gangs. At the same time, the political transition must proceed in tandem to ensure free, fair, and safe elections as soon as security conditions permit this. In view of the above, I would like to make three points. First, Greece appreciates the peaceful and timely transfer of executive power from the transitional presidential council to the council of ministers under Prime Minister Fisehmay. We reiterate our support for the prime minister and his priorities of restoring security and organizing elections. Any adjustments to the electoral calendar must aim solely at safeguarding optimal security conditions. We welcome the National Pact for Stability and the Organization of Elections and encourage all Haitian political stakeholders to endorse it, remaining genuinely committed to the political transition and contribute decisively to the efforts led by the Prime Minister to shape Haiti's next chapter. We further applaud the appointment of five women ministers following the cabinet reshuffle, a crucial step towards women's inclusive participation in the political process. We acknowledge the progress in the electoral preparations, most notably the registration of political parties, as credible elections remain the only path to restoring constitutional order. In this regard, I wish to emphasize the indispensable role of BINUH in supporting Haitian authorities throughout the transitional period, facilitating inter-Haitian political dialogue, and providing technical assistance for electoral preparations. Second, while anti-gang operations have achieved some tactical successes, primarily in the capital, the security situation remains fragile. Gangs continue to perpetrate killings, widespread human rights abuses, sexual and gender-based violence, and trafficking and recruitment of children. We repeat our strong condemnation of these atrocities and remain confident that the gradual deployment of the GSF will yield concrete security results. In this regard, yesterday we announced a financial contribution to the United Nations Trust Fund in support of the GSF. We commend all Member States that have pledged personnel to the GSF, while underscoring that all counter-gang operations must strictly adhere to international human rights standards to prevent excessive use of force. In parallel, we welcome the operationalization of UNSO and the appointment of Ms. Daniela Kroselak as its head, offering our unwavering support as she assumes this vital role. Third, Haiti remains one of the most dangerous places to be a child, with children comprising half of gang members and more than half a million displaced. Against this backdrop, we welcome the long-awaited reestablishment of the National Commission for Disarmament, Dismantlement, and Reintegration and the appointment of its members. We are hopeful that the reactivation of the commission will contribute to child recruitment prevention, violence reduction, and the design and implementation of safe exit and rehabilitation strategies for children and youth. At the same time, the justice system must be reformed to manage the projected increase in arrests following GSF deployment, with a specific focus on ending prolonged pre-trial detention, especially for children. Madam President, As Haiti is hopefully about to enter a new era with the gradual deployment of the GSF, Greece remains committed to supporting the nation's path towards security stabilization, a nationally owned democratic political transition, and sustainable development. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Greece for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Denmark.

Thank you, Madam President. And I also thank SRSD, Ruiz-Massieu, and GSF Special Representative Christofides for their briefings. And I welcome the participation of His Excellency, the Prime Minister, Fissamie, in this meeting. Today's briefing has detailed significant steps made in laying the foundation to restore Haiti's security, democracy, and rule of law. However, given the scale of Haiti's challenges, urgent progress is still needed. Madam President, with this in mind, allow me to make three points. First, Denmark remains alarmed by the dire security situation in Haiti. We welcome that the UN Support Office in Haiti became fully operational on 1 April. This office will be crucial in supporting international security assistance. We commend the UN for ensuring the timely opening of this office in line with Resolution 2793, despite the challenges in security and infrastructure. Denmark further welcomes the arrival of new personnel from Chad as part of the Gang Suppression Force and calls on Member States to accelerate and complete their deployment. All efforts, national and international, towards the establishment of security in Haiti must be undertaken in strict compliance with international law. We reiterate that the GSF must operate with the highest standard of conduct and discipline, with robust oversight and transparency. We are deeply alarmed by reports of accusations of sexual exploitation and abuse made against personnel in the Multinational Security Support Mission. All accusations must be thoroughly and objectively investigated and accountability ensured. We also underscore the need for the full implementation of the UN sanctions regime on Haiti, especially the arms embargo, to stem the flow of weapons exacerbating the security crisis. Second, Mr. President, Denmark remains deeply concerned by the catastrophic humanitarian and human rights situation in Haiti. More than half of Haiti's population is facing acute food insecurity, and over 6 million people require humanitarian assistance. Internal displacement continues to climb while access to basic services is collapsing. We call on Member States to scale up funding to Haiti's humanitarian response plan, which remains desperately underfunded. Human rights in Haiti continue to be under attack. Gangs commit widespread abuses, including killings, maiming, and trafficking. The scale and brutality of sexual and gender-based violence, including rape, is particularly alarming, with women and girls subjected to widespread and often systematic abuse. We strongly condemn all violations against children, including the sharp increase in recruitment by gangs. On this note, we welcome the reactivation of the National Commission for Disarmament, Dismantlement and Reintegration, and underline the need to advance a credible Haitian-led, DDR strategy. This must include viable pathways for disengagement, particularly for children and youth. Third, Mr. President, on the political situation, Denmark welcomes the peaceful transfer of executive authority on 7 February, following the expiration of the Transitional Presidential Council and the efforts to preserve institutional continuity. We take note of the National Pact for Stability and the organization of elections as an important Haitian-led initiative to advance the transition. We emphasize the need to translate commitments into concrete actions and encourage inclusive inter-Haitian dialogue to advance the political process. We acknowledge the progress made on electoral preparations and call on Haitian stakeholders to maintain momentum towards credible, inclusive and timely elections. This will require sustained political commitment, adequate financing and improved security conditions. Mr. President, in closing, Denmark reaffirms its strong commitment to the people of Haiti on their path to peace and security. The international community and this Council must remain steadfast in supporting Haitian-led efforts towards stability, rule of law, and a return to democratic government. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Denmark for the statement. I give the floor to the representative of Russian Federation.

Mr. President. We would like to thank the Special Representative of the Secretary-General, Carlos Ruiz Massieu, and the Special Representative for the Gang Suppression Force, Jack Christofides, for their briefings. We welcome to the meeting the Prime Minister of Haiti, Mr. Alix Didier Fisimil. The situation in this Caribbean state for some years now has been on the brink of disaster. However, The events of recent months, as noted in the briefers' statements, provide hope for a long-awaited end in the country to the spiral of violence and impunity that's been reigning. Whether this hope can be turned into lasting prospects to a large extent depends on successful presidential elections that should be a key step on the path to restoring constitutional order and legitimate authorities in the country. We note the measures taken by the transitional government to prepare for the elections, and we trust that the vote will be organised, if not in strict compliance with the initial plans, then as soon as possible. The Haitians need international support to organize and conduct the elections, and this role has recently become the focus of the mandate of BINUH, the UN Integrated Office in Haiti. We are convinced that under the leadership of Carlos Ruiz Massieu, and in coordination with the other international presences in the country, the UN Special Political Mission will provide Port-au-Prince with as much assistance as possible. However, there is a need to completely avoid external interference in the electoral process itself after two centuries of colonial intervention, blackmail, demeaning reparations and predatory loans. Haitians deserve the opportunity to determine their own future by themselves. The main issue is to ensure security for a representative vote. The numerous gangs, despite the heroic efforts of the Haitian police, continue to maintain brutal control over a significant part of the country and its population. They are still, unhindered, buying weapons smuggled from the US, ignoring the arms embargo that only functions nominally. In order to dislodge the gangs from their embedded positions, the island has seen the start of the deployment of the Gang Suppression Force and UNSO. We recognise the prompt and effective actions of the standing group of partners and the secretariat, which have enabled conditions to be put in place for the arrival on the island of the first troops this month. We are grateful to all TCCs for their resolve to help the Haitians. However, it is clear that the deployment of the GSF in Haiti is not going to be a walk in the park. gang members will inevitably mount fierce resistance, and the new troops will face real ordeals in the future in the country. Given the arrival of the first units of the force and the high hopes pinned on them, I'd like to point out two points. Firstly, given the parallel withdrawal of the Kenyan troops from Haiti, A situation might occur whereby the number of GSF personnel is even lower than the 1,000 personnel who were deployed as part of the previous Multinational Security Support Mission. It is important to prevent a security vacuum and reversals in the fragile results achieved by the troops under the leadership of Nairobi. Secondly, the GSF. was given a very broad and vague mandate for the use of force, which, inter alia, meant that we were not able at the time to support the resolution on its establishment. I'm not going to get into the details, but the CONOPS and the rules for the use of force by which the mission is guided, we're assured will be used responsibly, but we'd like to draw attention to the crucial need to respect the rights of and to protect the lives of Haitian civilians and primarily children. Many of them, unfortunately, have been recruited into criminal gangs and are going to fire at peacekeepers. And this will raise the difficult challenge of choosing how to respond to and properly treat minors. We see the potential here for joint work between Port-au-Prince and the international presences in Haiti, first and foremost, as part of the recently established National Commission on Disarmament and dismantling of armed groups and reintegration. The potential violations in this area would leave a stain on the reputation of the entire international community and the UN Security Council, which set up the mission. In this regard, Russia, as a permanent member of the Security Council, is going to continue to closely monitor the progress in operationalizing the GSF and will ensure due international control for its work. I thank you.
I thank the representative of the Russian Federation for the statement. I shall now make a statement in my capacity as the representative of Bahrain.

Excellencies, allow me to welcome His Excellency Alex Didier Felix Fisselme, Prime Minister of Haiti, in our session today. I would also like to thank the Secretary-General for his report. And I thank Mr. Carlos Ruiz Massieu, the Special Representative of the Secretary-General and head of the United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti. I also thank Mr. Jack Christofides, the Special Representative for the Gang Suppression Force, for their valuable briefings. I also welcome the permanent representatives of the Dominican Republic, the Trinidad and Tobago, Kenya, and the permanent observer of the International Organization of the Francophonie. The Kingdom of Bahrain is following the political, security, and humanitarian situations in Haiti. In light of the Secretary-General report on Haiti, I would like to stress three key points. One, we welcome the Haitian efforts in holding the consultations with all the relevant parties, which led to the signing of the national Charter and the National Pact for Stability, which is a national track for holding free and credible elections that could lead to security and stability in the country. This is a political initiative led by Haitians. We also welcome the recent ministerial amendment, which led to the appointment of five women ministers. The percentage of women representation increased to 28 percent. This proves that the role of women is being promoted in the political process. Two, we stress the need to continue making every effort to ensure security, the rule of law, and fighting violence by gangs. in order to ensure compliance with international humanitarian standards. We also welcome the efforts of the Gang Suppression Force, and we stress the need to continue its deployment and to promote its readiness -- operational readiness to support national authorities in fighting security challenges and contributing to the protection of civilians, stability, and sustainable security, while preventing the recurrence of conflicts. Three, we stress the importance of collective international efforts and working with the UN Support Office in Haiti, as well as the Gang Suppression Force, to support Haiti and support its people in countering these challenges in order to ensure its security and promote development and peace. This could also help in alleviating the continued violence and preventing the forced recruitment of children, as well as internal displacement and food insecurity. We also stress our support to the UN Integrated Office in Haiti in its work to promote the political process and accelerate the preparations for the elections. In conclusion, we renew our solidarity with the Republic of Haiti and its people. We stress that we are committed to working together with the international community and the United Nations to overcome the current challenges and ensure a safer, more stable future for the friendly Haitian people. I resume my function as a President of the Council. I now give the floor to His Excellency, Mr. Alex Tede Fils-Aime, Prime Minister of the Republic of Haiti.

Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, members of the Council, first and foremost, I would like to express my sincere gratitude to the Ambassador of the Kingdom of Bahrain and the President of the Council for this opportunity that has been given to me to speak to this august Assembly. Your commitment to peace remains a source of hope for Haiti. I would also like to thank the members of the Council for the ongoing attention given to the situation in Haiti. Holding this special session since the Gang Suppression Force was deployed on 1 April illustrates the resolve of the international community to assist Haiti in this profound crisis. I welcome the efforts of the Secretary-General, Mr. Antonio Guterres, and report S/2026/325 of 14 April 2026. This highlights the complex nature of the situation, but also the resilience of the Haitian people given insecurity. I would also like to thank the Special Representative in Haiti, Ambassador Carlos Ruiz Massieu, for the excellent quality of his work. I would also like to express the gratitude of the Haitian people to those Member States who have taken the floor today. Their contributions enlighten our shared action. I would like to assure this Council that all comments made have been duly taken into consideration. The Transition Government remains fully committed to help Haiti emerge from this crisis. Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen. I would like to bring to you a simple message that has already been conveyed to the Haitian people on the 7th of February. The time has come to come together. The state is taking up its rightful place again. Haiti shall not perish. This message reflects the resolve of the Haitian political forces to work together, as demonstrated by the Pact for Stability and the Organization of Elections. The transition government has three priorities: restoring the authority of the state, protecting the population, and preparing the return for constitutional order. We have a deep conviction, without security, no development is possible. Specific results are starting to emerge. Thanks to the Haitian armed forces, the National Police and the Gang Suppression Force, several areas in the capital are slowly being retaken. Economic and social life is slowly but surely starting up again. There is an absolute need for urgency. The deployment of the GSF must take place without delay. while we are also acting on the medium term. However, in the immediate term, strengthening the HNP with the P4000 project is underway. 1,200 police officers have already been made operational, 887 additional. Ones are going to be deployed shortly with a objective of 2,500 to 3,000 by the end of 2026 in terms of the Haitian Armed Forces. Progress is speeding up. 338 new soldiers trained at the Vertier base will have graduated on the, will graduate rather, on the 21st of April. For some two weeks now, 200 servicemen have been involved in consolidating the areas retaken by the HNP in the center of Port-au-Prince. In six weeks time, Vertier may well welcome 400 new recruits out of the 770 that have been waiting for two months. In 10 weeks time, the Anacona base, the second training center, may well welcome 300 new recruits. If the work makes progress as planned, in the next six months, the Haitian armed forces may include about 700 additional service personnel. These, added to the 200 who are already involved in rebuilding, will be the first troop of elite troops of the army. A new doctrine for the Haitian armed forces is also being drafted. A letter to request technical support has been sent to the permanent representative of Haiti to call on to call for assistance and from the Inter-American Defense Center, a working group made-up of and this is for the permanent representative of the OAS, a working group composed of legal experts and defense experts has been set up within the defense ministry to achieve this work. This is why we fully support the recommendations of the Secretary General in terms of strengthening the mission. In all operations conducted, the respect for human rights recalls for is absolutely fundamental measures have been taken to protect civilians and avoid all abuse amongst the armed groups the gangs that continue to refuse to lay down their arms I reiterate justice will be brought whilst respecting human dignity and respecting the laws in force Mr. President There are two strategic areas that are guiding our action: the Palm-Miraguan region in the Greater South and the Haut-Plateau Central or Artibonite for the Greater North. These corridors are not just security corridors; they are seeking to re-establish traffic, support the economy, and strengthen the state's presence. There has been mass displacement of the population, and so the government has started a program of voluntary return to people's homes in order to restore dignity and stability for families. This process is also assisting the preparation of the electoral process. Progress has been made. The legal context is there, political parties are on the lists, and the electoral budget has been prepared. Our aim remains unchanged: to restore citizens' trust in democratic institutions. Mr. President, I am delighted that there has been the official resumption of dialogue with the Dominican Republic. This is based on mutual respect and peaceful cooperation. In conclusion, The Republic of Haiti calls upon the Security Council and the United Nations to further, swiftly and concretely support the deployment of the gang suppression force, in particular in financial and logistical terms. The Haitian people is not asking for charity. We are asking for solidarity and for means to rebuild our future. Haiti is resisting. Haiti is recovering. Haiti will survive. I thank you.
I thank His Excellency Mr. Faisandier for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Dominican Republic.

Mr. President, Your Excellency, Mr. Alix Didier Fisseme, Prime Minister of the Republic of Haiti, Mr. Carlos Ruiz Massieu, Special Representative of the Secretary General, Mr. Jack

Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the 14 member states of the Caribbean Community, CARICOM. There has been institutional progress, and some security gains. Notwithstanding, Mr. President, CARICOM remains deeply concerned by the ongoing security challenges, governance challenges, and worsening humanitarian situation in Haiti. The expansion of gang control continues, while incidents of sexual violence, fatalities, child and children recruitment, internal displacement, kidnapping, extortion, and food insecurity are all on the rise. Mister President, the situation remains dire. And is challenged daily. The Caribbean community has focused its efforts on supporting the establishment and the work of the now dissolved transitional presidential council. as well as the Haiti Good Offices Mechanism through the CARICOM Endorsed Eminent Persons Group. At this juncture, Mr. President, CARICOM takes this opportunity to express its appreciation to the Government of Kenya, the United States, and all participating countries for their commitment and support to Haiti as it confronts a complex, multidimensional security crisis. With the establishment and operationalization of the United Nations Support Office in Haiti, To assist the work of the Gang Suppression Force, and with the recent renewal of the mandate of the United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti, which the CARICOM Caucus of Ambassadors here in New York welcomed in this chamber on January 29th, there is a meaningful opportunity to generate positive and sustained outcomes in support of stability and institutional strengthening in Haiti. with all three mechanisms working in unison. Most pressing for CARICOM, however, are the first round of general elections scheduled for August 2026 and the second round scheduled for December 2026, as well as the progress of the GSF and the Haitian National Police in improving the security environment necessary for elections to take place. CARICOM reaffirms its unwavering solidarity with the people of Haiti. Mr. President, we urge this Council to remain seized of the matter and to act with unity and resolve for a stable Haiti in the short term and a lasting, peaceful solution in the medium to long term. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the representative of Trinidad and Tobago for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Kenya.

Thank you, Mr. President. I commend you and, through you, the delegation of the Kingdom of Bahrain for the exemplary stewardship of the Security Council during the month of April. I thank SRS G Carlos Ruiz Massieu and the Special Representative of the Gang Suppression Force, Mr. Jack Christofides, for their comprehensive briefings on the current situation in Haiti. I acknowledge with gratitude the participation of His Excellency Alex Didier Phils-Aime, the Prime Minister of Haiti, and his delegation. I commend all members of this Security Council for their continued and unequivocal commitment to the people of Haiti. Over the past six months, the Council has adopted key resolutions including 2793, establishing the Gang Suppression Force; 2795, renewing the sanctions regime; and 2814, revising and extending the mandate of BINUH. These measures underscore the Council's sustained resolve to support Haiti's path toward stability and recovery. Mr. President, the situation in Haiti remains deeply concerning. It is still fragile and marked by protracted gang violence beyond the capital. Yet, even amid these challenges, hope endures, rooted in the resilience of the Haitian people, the determination of their leadership to restore state authority and democratic governance, and the steadfast support of the international community. This briefing therefore takes place at a pivotal point. Today, Haiti stands at a critical juncture in its stabilization process. Currently, the transition from the Multinational Security Support Mission, MSS, to the Gang Suppression Force, GSF, is approaching its completion. The deployment and operations of the MSS which commenced in June 2024, has demonstrated that the mission for restoration of security to Haiti is possible. Mr. President, as the Council will recall, in 2023, Kenya responded to the call of the Haitian people and the international community to help address entrenched gang violence threatening to further destabilize an already fragile socioeconomic and political environment with broader implications for the Caribbean region. In his address to the General Assembly in September 2023, the President of the Republic of Kenya, President William Ruto, pledged to deploy 1,000 officers to the envisioned 2,500-strong MSS mission, a commitment that was subsequently operationalized through Security Council Resolution 2699 of 2023. Kenya further accepted to take the leadership of the mission, provided the force commander, and the largest number of the fighting force. Under Kenya's leadership, the mission has adhered strictly to its guiding frameworks, including the concept of operations, the Status of Forces Agreement, and the UN Human Rights Due Diligence Policy, upholding the highest standards of professionalism, accountability, and transparency. My delegation commends the courage and professionalism of the Haitian National Police, alongside MSS contingents from Kenya, the Bahamas, Belize, Canada, El Salvador, Guatemala, and Jamaica, who have served with distinction under extremely challenging conditions. Mr. President, let me address an issue which has been alluded to by the delegation of Panama and Denmark. In August 2025, allegations of sexual exploitation and abuse relating to the conduct of some MSS personnel as referenced in the Secretary General's report were reported. The MSS leadership acted promptly by establishing a board of inquiry. The findings of that board were formally communicated to the Inspector General of the Haitian National Police and relevant United Nations human rights structures in Haiti. Those findings are unfortunately inconsistent with the avowments in the Secretary General's report. And the government of the Republic of Kenya has written formally to the Secretary General in that regard. But let me be clear, Mr. President. Kenya reaffirms its commitment to the highest standards of conduct, transparency, and accountability. This commitment has guided our participation in and leadership of peacekeeping missions across the world for decades, and we shall not waver in that endeavor. Kenya therefore remains prepared to cooperate fully with the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights and other relevant mechanisms, including in consideration of any subsequently emerging relevant and credible information. Mr. President, although the mission faced significant personnel, logistical, and material constraints, it demonstrated and surpassed professionalism. In close coordination with the Haitian National Police, MSS forces conducted targeted anti-gang operations, contributing to measurable gains. Most notably, they secured and protected strategic infrastructure, including the seat of government, the airport and seaport, as well as the main supply roads, facilitated humanitarian access, and ensured the delivery of essential services, including healthcare and education. They have also contributed to restoring security, particularly in parts of Port-au-Prince, and to gradual revival of economic activity in areas that were previously under gun control. Most fundamentally, these efforts have supported governmental continuity through multiple transitions, the most notable being the 7th February 2026 transition that led to a consolidation of authority going forward. We also honor the memory of MSS officers, Mr. Samuel Tomoi, Mr. Benedict Kabiru, and Mr. Kennedy Nzuve, who made the ultimate sacrifice in the line of duty. Mr. President, the progress achieved by a contingent of 999 personnel demonstrates that stability in Haiti is possible. Persuaded of this, Kenya has and will remain a strong advocate for stronger international support for Haiti that is clearly mandated, adequately resourced, and effectively coordinated. It's therefore imperative that the GSF is fully operationalized and sufficiently resourced. This will require collective action through timely implementation, sustained political commitment, and predictable, adequate financing to ensure that the mission delivers tangible and lasting impact. This moment is particularly critical as the last fighting contingent of the MSS departs from theater at the end of April 2026. In the last six months, Kenya has been part of the standing group of partners that has been engaged in the various aspects of the standing of the GSF. And during that time, and in line with the commitment of His Excellency President William Ruto to the international community, Kenya has been engaged in a process that guarantees an orderly transition and transfer of responsibilities in line with the evolving mission framework. We have provided leadership and operational support during this transition, laying the foundation for a more capable and better resourced GSF able to effectively deliver on its mandate. We believe that the MSS experience and successes attained provide a strong foundation upon which the GSF should build. Mr. President, as I conclude, I extend the sincere appreciation of my country and my delegation to all stakeholders that are engaged in this effort, including troop-contributing and police-contributing countries and all donors, both bilateral as well as those that contribute through the UN Trust Fund. I also thank the Secretary-General for his leadership in establishing and operationalizing the trust fund, as well as for his comprehensive report on enhancing the United Nations role in Haiti. The recommendations therein, informed by lessons from the MSS, have been reflected in the design of the GSF and the revised mandate of BINU, and will continue to guide stabilization efforts. Finally, I reaffirm Kenya's unwavering solidarity with the people of Haiti. While our troop deployment is concluding as part of the MSS to GSF transition, our commitment remains steadfast. Kenya will continue to engage constructively with Haiti and international partners in support of stabilization, recovery and the restoration of lasting peace and security. Thank you, Mr. President.

The Francophonie, with its special relationship to Haiti, is mobilized to support this dynamic in a determined manner, and we are committed through our concrete support to the new architecture of the gang suppression force. And it is in this spirit that the Francophonie has continued to provide support to the political process through visits from the special envoy of the Secretary General of the Francophonie, Mr. Domitien Ndisaye. And the OIF also provides technical support to the electoral process by upholding the organ to manage elections, promoting an inclusive process for vulnerable groups, and supporting national electoral observation, as well as information integrity and the fight against corruption. These crucial efforts demand better international mobilization and better coordination.

And in this dynamic, the Secretary General of the Francophonie, Madame Louise Mushikwabo, keeps a regular channel of dialogue open with all regional.

Partners, such as the Secretary General of CARICOM and the Secretary General of OAS.

We are, of course, convinced that it will be Haitian men and women who will lead this process and will fully assume their responsibilities. Mr. President, the multidimensional crisis in Haiti also.

Compels us to pay special attention to the human dimension of it. Violence, especially sexual and gender-based violence, has reached an alarming level, and women and girls are at the front line of this.

Supporting victims, access to justice, economic empowerment, as well as the full and complete participation of women in the political process and in public.

Life are essential levers in order to strengthen the resilience of communities.

We are convinced of the pivotal role that Haitian women can play in a return to political, social and security stability. So the OIF has included Haiti as a priority country in the fund, the Francophonie Stands with Women. 36 initiatives led by Haitian women have been supported through this mechanism for solidarity for a total amount of 2.3 million euros and 11 new projects have benefited from additional support of around 1 million euros in the framework of the sixth round of funding provided by this fund and there was a partnership concluded in November 2025.

With UN Women in Haiti, this was essential to identify these initiatives and make sure that follow-up was provided. Mr. President, to conclude, it is important to underline that this current moment demands that we are lucid and determined.

Lucid because the challenges are considerable and the achievements are fragile, and determined because we have an open window of opportunity. and we should make the most out of it to ensure security in the country and ensure the necessary conditions for a credible electoral process. This means reestablishing security.

As well as state functions, and to open up a democratic horizon and give a renewed outlook to the Haitian population.

The Francophonie is ready to continue and to strengthen its commitment to support the efforts of the Haitian authorities and the international community, and we will continue to fully assume our political responsibility toward Haiti with solidarity, a Member State with which it shares a history, a language, values, and a deep aspiration for peace.
